source.title: Interpretable Physics Reasoning and Performance Taxonomy in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Pranav Pawar; Kavish Shah; Akshat Bhalani; Komal Kasat; Devanshu Mittal; Hadi Gala; Deepali Patil; Nikita Raichada; M. Deshmukh

record.tranche_reason: Extends the scale–performance question to vision-language models evaluated on physics reasoning, a new model type and task setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream physics-task scores for four models of different parameter counts, so those scores bear on V6. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, or run compute-budget allocation experiments. Cited scaling laws and prompting choices are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream physics-benchmark scores of four VLMs from different families (1.3B to 27B) and reads them as a scale–performance relation. That bears on V6 in a new setting, but only weakly: size is confounded with family, data and training, there are just four points, and nothing is related to pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. The authors claim a strong positive correlation between model size and physics reasoning and say continued scaling remains viable. They also note that the 7B Qwen beating the 11B LLaMA suggests architecture may override size, and that domain variation calls for architectural innovation. Their own Table 1 overall ranking (7B > 11B > 27B > 1.3B) does not show the claimed correlation; the paraphrase should say so.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates downstream physics-task scores across selected VLMs; it does not measure held-out language-model loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Model ranking and scores vary across physics domains and metrics; the authors specifically note Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforming the larger LLaMA-3.2-Vision-11B overall.
record.problems: Only four differently named model families are compared; parameter count is not varied in a controlled within-family scaling series, and the study measures task scores rather than pretraining loss. Confidence intervals are reported for overall scores, but not for the separate physics-accuracy, reasoning-quality, or domain scores.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 efficiency measurements, quantization statements in Section 4.5, and qualitative examples are not direct measures of the scale–performance relation in V6. Cited scaling-law results are not this study's findings.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss; a controlled within-family size series; any fitted functional form or forecast of downstream scores.
All parts: no pretraining loss and no power-law fits.
All parts: no controlled shape comparison.
All parts: no loss power law in another modality or training regime.
All parts: no comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Error analysis: computational errors more common in smaller models (23% vs 12%); conceptual errors make up 52–67% of failures. The comparison groups are not specified.
Pairwise significance: all overall-score pairs significant; some domain comparisons not significant (Fluid, Qwen-7B vs LLaMA-11B).

record.verdict_notes: Data reliability is doubtful. 'Gemma2-27B-Vision' is not a standard released model. Several text statements contradict the tables: the text says Gemma achieved the highest accuracy while ranking it third overall, and calls Mechanics challenging with the same 0.79 average as the 'strong' domains. Stated significance also conflicts with the large Fluid gap. Many references appear mis-attributed. Treat all V6 verdicts as low-weight: four cross-family models, size confounded with architecture and data, no pretraining loss. Table 3 efficiency and the quantization results are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates VLMs on a visual physics task but does not test whether a pretraining-loss power law holds across modalities or training regimes.
Tests physics-task performance across different model sizes; does not test predictability from pretraining loss or across a controlled scaling series.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or curve shapes.

relationships.condition: Reasoning-quality metric across the four VLMs
relationships.reason: Reasoning quality rises monotonically with stated size, 0.69→0.78→0.83→0.85 (r9–r12). This is cross-family, with only four points.
relationships.display_finding: Reasoning quality increased from 0.69 to 0.78 to 0.83 to 0.85 across four models from different families.

relationships.condition: Overall composite score, models of 7B and larger
relationships.reason: Overall score falls with size above 7B: 7B 0.815 > 11B 0.765 > 27B 0.75, with non-overlapping CIs (r2–r4).
relationships.display_finding: Composite scores fell from 0.815 at 7B to 0.765 at 11B and 0.75 at 27B, with nonoverlapping confidence intervals.

relationships.reason: The largest model is best and the smallest worst in most metrics and domains, but the 11B model trails the 7B model everywhere, and 7B is top in Fluid Dynamics (r5–r8, r13–r28).
relationships.display_finding: The largest model usually led and the smallest usually trailed, yet 11B underperformed 7B everywhere and 7B led Fluid Dynamics.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: DeepSeek-VL-1.3B compared with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on overall score
reader_labels.reason: The 7B model scores 0.815 versus 0.70 for the 1.3B model, consistent with better downstream performance at larger scale (r1–r2).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Overall scores for Qwen2.5-VL-7B compared with LLaMA-3.2-Vision-11B and Gemma2-27B-Vision
reader_labels.reason: Both larger models score below the 7B Qwen model, so the results do not show a consistent improvement with increasing parameter count (r2–r4).
